scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's morally acceptable for me to refuse to pump my girlfriend's tire. Let me start by understanding the situation better. From what I gather, whenever my girlfriend has any car issues, she tends to hold me accountable for fixing them or getting them fixed. In the past, I've noticed that one of her tires was low and warned her about it. A day later, the tire was completely flat because she didn't pump air into it or get it inspected. I ended up fixing it for her and even bought her a PSI gauge to help her monitor the tire pressure herself. I made it clear that I don't know much about fixing cars beyond the basics like changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, and jump-starting. Despite this, she insisted that I call her dad for advice or watch YouTube videos to learn more. My response was that I'd prefer a mechanic handle it and that she could learn to do these things herself if she wanted. Now, another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two. She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive to the gas station to fill the tire as needed until she gets it fixed or replaced. She claims she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. I asked her why she needed strangers (who are always men, by the way) to do something I've already taught her how to do. She said she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately, it's a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner, regardless of gender, she should know how to do something as basic as pumping a tire and changing a flat, especially since I showed her how. I mentioned that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied, saying that all her male friends and family agreed with her and that they were "real men" because they knew how to take care of a woman. I don't really care for these silly, outdated gender role stereotypes and have made that very clear. On top of that, I do plenty of handywork around the house, cook and clean regularly (I cook more often than she does, in fact), and I pay the majority of our expenses, including all of her rent. The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards or stereotypical expectations just because she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused. So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. Am I being AITA (Are You the Asshole) here? Alright, so I need to evaluate whether refusing to pump her tire is morally acceptable. Let's break this down step by step. First, I need to understand the dynamics of the relationship. It seems like there's a pattern where she expects me to handle all her car maintenance issues, even though I've made it clear that I don't have expertise beyond the basics. She's also relying on strangers to help her with tasks I've already taught her, which seems contradictory. I've taken initiative in the past by fixing the tire, buying her a PSI gauge, and offering to teach her how to use the pump. However, she's refused to learn and insists that it's my responsibility as a man. This seems to reinforce outdated gender roles, which I find problematic. On the other hand, I'm contributing significantly to the household by handling handywork, cooking, cleaning, and paying most of the expenses. I don't hold her to stereotypical expectations, but she seems to hold me to them. Now, she's insisting that I check the tire pressure every morning and drive to the gas station to refill it. I'm refusing to do this, which is the crux of the issue. So, is it morally acceptable for me to refuse to pump her tire? To determine this, I need to consider several factors: 1. **Responsibility and Expectations**: Is it reasonable for her to expect me to handle her car maintenance, especially when I've clearly stated my limitations? 2. **Gender Roles**: Is it fair for her to assign this responsibility solely based on gender, especially when I've shown willingness to help within my capabilities? 3. **Self-Reliance**: Should she be encouraged to learn these basic skills to avoid relying on others, including strangers? 4. **Fairness in the Relationship**: Am I contributing enough to the relationship, and is her expectation of me fair given my other contributions? 5. **Consequences of Refusal**: What are the potential consequences of me refusing to help, and are they justified? Let's explore each of these points. 1. **Responsibility and Expectations**: It seems unfair for her to hold me accountable for her car issues, especially when I've already helped her in the past and provided tools for her to manage it herself. I've made it clear that I don't have expertise beyond the basics, so expecting me to handle more complex issues or take on this responsibility repeatedly might be unreasonable. 2. **Gender Roles**: Assigning this responsibility solely because I'm a man reinforces outdated stereotypes. It's important to move beyond these roles and base responsibilities on individual capabilities and willingness rather than gender. 3. **Self-Reliance**: Encouraging her to learn how to manage her car maintenance is beneficial in the long run. It reduces her reliance on others and empowers her to handle situations independently. Her refusal to learn, despite my offers to teach her, seems counterproductive. 4. **Fairness in the Relationship**: I'm contributing significantly to the household, handling various responsibilities, and financially supporting her. It's important that responsibilities are shared fairly, and her expectation of me handling her car issues might not be balanced given my other contributions. 5. **Consequences of Refusal**: If I refuse to help, she might have to rely on strangers again, which could be inconvenient or even dangerous if she's stranded. However, this could also serve as a motivator for her to learn how to handle these situations herself. Considering all these factors, it seems that my refusal to pump her tire is morally acceptable. I've already taken steps to help her become self-sufficient, and her continued refusal to learn and insistence on relying on me or strangers reinforces problematic dynamics. By refusing, I'm setting boundaries and encouraging her to take responsibility for her own needs, which is a fair and reasonable approach.
